## Other sources of information

This vignette is an expansion of the ["Data" section](https://noaa-fims.github.io/FIMS/articles/fims-demo.html#data) in the [FIMS overview vignette](https://noaa-fims.github.io/FIMS/articles/fims-demo.html). It provides more details about the data structure needed for a FIMS model and how to prepare your data for use in a FIMS model using the `FIMSFrame()` function.

The [FIMS cheatsheet](https://github.com/NOAA-FIMS/FIMS/tree/main/pkgdown/assets/fims-cheatsheet.pdf) includes a quick summary of the input data format.

The help page for the `FIMS::data_big` data set (https://noaa-fims.github.io/FIMS/reference/data_big.html or via `?FIMS::data_big`) provides detailed information about the input data format.

Note: this vignette does not include anything about model configuration, which is covered in the overview vignette linked above.

## Data format

The input data for a FIMS model is a single long data frame with the following columns: `r glue::glue_collapse(colnames(FIMS::data_big), sep = ", ", last = ", and ")`. Both the single table and long format are in contrast to the input format for some legacy stock assessment models where the data are provided in multiple tables, each with a different format. The SS3 data file, for instance, has separate tables for catch, indices, age compositions, length compositions, with wide tables for the composition data (each age or length bin has a different column). The use of a single, long table for data input used by FIMS makes it easier to summarize and filter the data across data types (e.g., by fleet, timing, age, etc.), as well as being better suited to the widely-used tidyverse collection of packages in R.

Two drawbacks of the long format are (1) some information is duplicated, and (2) the long format is harder to read and understand by looking at the raw data frame. To meet this second challenge, the FIMS team is working on functions to summarize, visualize, and check for errors in the input data.

The currently available values for the `type` column are `r glue::glue_collapse(glue::glue('\"{FIMS::fims_input_types}\"'), sep = ", ", last = ", and ")`. The "weight_at_age", "spawning_weight_at_age", "fecundity_at_age", "maturity_at_age", "fecundity_at_length", "maturity_at_length", and "age_to_length_conversion" types are not currently treated as data in the sense that they are not included in the likelihood, just used within the population dynamics calculations.

The individual data types are described in more detail below after introducing the example data set that is included in the package.

## `data_big`

A sample data frame for a catch-at-age model with both ages and lengths is stored in the package as `data_big`. This data set is based on data that was used in [Li et al. (2021)](https://www.doi.org/10.7755/FB.119.2-3.5) for the Model Comparison Project ([github site](https://github.com/NOAA-FIMS/Age_Structured_Stock_Assessment_Model_Comparison)). The length data have since been added [data-raw/data_big.R](https://github.com/NOAA-FIMS/FIMS/blob/main/data-raw/data_big.R) based on an age--length conversion matrix. To see how this example data frame was created, see the R script here [R/data_big.R](https://github.com/NOAA-FIMS/FIMS/blob/main/R/data_big.R).

## `FIMSFrame()`

`FIMSFrame()` must be used to create a data object that can be passed to a FIMS model. This function returns an object that has the `FIMSFrame` class. This class contains a data slot that stores the input data frame and several other slots that store summary information about the object, e.g., the fleet names, the number of age bins, etc. All of this information can be accessed using `get_*()` functions, e.g., `get_n_years()`, `get_fleets()`. Every fleet named in the data must have catch, index, or composition data. `FIMSFrame()` returns an error otherwise, so a misspelled fleet name in other rows does not add a fleet to the model.

When you execute `FIMSFrame()` on a long data frame, such as `data_big`, the function executes several error checks to help ensure that your data is ready for a FIMS model. For example, until the internal estimation of growth is possible, all catch-at-age models require weight-at-age data. If your data frame does not have weight-at-age data, then `FIMSFrame()` will error and return helpful information on what you are missing.

The output of `FIMSFrame()` also contains summary information about your data and has an internal plotting function. See the [FIMS overview vignette](https://noaa-fims.github.io/FIMS/articles/fims-demo.html) for more information.

```{r fims-frame}
data_4_model <- FIMSFrame(data_big)
data_4_model
```

## Catch (`type == "catch"`)

The catch data type contains the total catch in weight or numbers for each time step. FIMS does not yet include the option to model discards internally, so "catch" should account for all catch. The catch are not associated with an age or length so those columns should only contain `NA` values. The `unit` column should be `mt` for catch in weight or `number` for catch in numbers, and all catch rows of a fleet must use the same unit. FIMS fits `mt` catch to the expected catch in weight and `number` catch to the expected catch in numbers. FIMS does not rescale catch, so catch in numbers must be on the same scale as numbers at age in the model. For example, when weight at age is in mt per fish, catch in numbers is the number of fish, not thousands of fish. The `uncertainty` column should be the standard deviation of the logged observations if you are using the lognormal distribution to fit your data. `log_Fmort` parameters for each fleet and time step with catch can be estimated to fit the model to the catch data, informed by the uncertainty values. Common practice is to set the uncertainty to a small number, like 0.001, so the catch data are fit closely. A catch of 0 means the fleet did not fish in that time step. `setup_default_parameters()` fixes `log_Fmort` for that fleet and year at -200, so fishing mortality is effectively 0, and the 0 is left out of the likelihood. It is reported as -999 in the output, the same as missing data. If you estimate `log_Fmort` in that year instead, `initialize_fims()` warns, because nothing in the data informs it. A fleet with a catch of 0 in every year and no composition data gives no information on its selectivity. Use -999, not 0, for a missing catch.

```{r data_big-catch}
# first three rows of the catch data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "catch") |>
  head(3)
```

```{r data_big-catch-plot}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Barplot shows an increase in catch over the timing values 1 to 8, then noisy but stable values until the final bar at timing equals 30.
# time series plot of catch data
library(ggplot2)
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "catch") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = timing, y = observed)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  ggtitle("Catch time series in data_big example data set")
```

## Indices (`type == "index"`)

The index data type contains the relative or absolute abundance index for each time step. The inputs are similar to catch, in having `NA` values for age and length, `mt` or `number` for `unit` (1 unit for all index rows of a fleet), and index uncertainty as the standard deviation of the logged observations. An index of 0 or less cannot be fit with the lognormal distribution, and `FIMSFrame()` returns an error for it. Use -999 for a missing index, or a distribution that allows 0.

```{r data_big-indices}
# first three rows of the index data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "index") |>
  head(3)
```

```{r data_big-indices-plot}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Points with uncertainty shows a steadily decreasing index over time steps 1 to 30 with increasing precision for the later observations.
# time series plot of index data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "index") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = timing, y = observed)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(ggplot2::aes(
    ymin = stats::qlnorm(
      p = 0.025,
      meanlog = log(observed),
      sdlog = unlist(
        FIMS:::parse_data_distribution(uncertainty)$sdlog,
        use.names = FALSE
      )
    ),
    ymax = stats::qlnorm(
      p = 0.975,
      meanlog = log(observed),
      sdlog = unlist(
        FIMS:::parse_data_distribution(uncertainty)$sdlog,
        use.names = FALSE
      )
    )
  )) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle("Index time series in data_big example data set")
```

## Age compositions (`type == "age_comp"`)

The age-composition data type contains the age distribution of a fleet for a time step. The `age` column contains integer ages defining the age bins. While standard FIMS models typically assume age bins start at zero, the data_big example currently uses ages ranging from 1--12, and thus, recruitment will be age-1 fish not age-0 fish. The `observed` column contains either the number or the proportion of the catch or survey in each age bin. The `unit` column should be either "number" or "proportion". If "proportion" is used, the observations are checked at a later step to confirm that they sum to 1.0. The `uncertainty` column should be the input sample size for the time step (equal across all ages within that time step). When the unit is set to a proportion, the sample size is multiplied by the proportion; however, when it is set to a number, the sample size is ignored.

```{r data_big-age_comp}
# first three rows of the age composition data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_comp") |>
  head(3)
```
```{r data_big-age_comp-plot}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Barplot showing age comp by time step with a larger proportion of older ages (including a significant plus group at age 12 for the early time steps) and a truncated age distribution in the final time steps with relatively few fish over age 7.
# plot of age compositions by time step
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_comp") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = age, y = observed)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  ggplot2::xlab("Age") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Number") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~timing) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = get_ages(data_4_model)) +
  ggtitle("Age compositions by time step in data_big example data set")
```

## Length compositions (`type == "length_comp"`)

The length-composition data are similar to the age compositions, except with values in the `length` column and `age = NA`. The `length` column identifies the length bin for each observation by its lower edge. A bin holds lengths from its lower edge up to the next lower edge. For example, with `length` values of 0, 50, ..., 1100, the bin labeled `250` includes fish measuring at least 250 mm but less than 300 mm (250–299 mm for whole-number measurements). The next bin, labeled `300`, includes fish measuring at least 300 mm but less than 350 mm (i.e. `[300, 350)` in interval notation). When growth is estimated in FIMS, the first bin also holds all smaller fish and the last bin holds all larger fish. With fixed `age_to_length_conversion` rows, those rows set what each bin holds. The `observed` column contains either the number or the proportion of fish in each length bin. The `unit` column should be either "number" or "proportion". The `uncertainty` column should be the input sample size for the time step, repeated across all length bins in that time step. When the unit is set to a proportion, the sample size is multiplied by the proportion; however, when it is set to a number, the sample size is ignored.

When length compositions are included, FIMS needs a way to convert numbers at age into numbers at length. This can come from fixed `age_to_length_conversion` rows or from a growth-derived age-to-length conversion using the VonB-Schnute Growth module.

```{r data_big-length_comp}
# first three rows of the length composition data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "length_comp") |>
  head(3)
```
```{r data_big-length_comp-plot}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Barplot showing length comp by time step with a mode around 450 mm which declines and becomes more sharply peaked over time.
# plot of length compositions by time step
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "length_comp") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = length, y = observed)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  ggplot2::xlab("Length") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Number") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~timing) +
  ggtitle("Length compositions by time step in data_big example data set")
```

## Length bins (`type == "length_bin"`)

The `length_bin` data type defines length bins without providing length-composition observations. These rows are useful when a model needs length-bin geometry for a growth-derived age-to-length conversion, but the user is not fitting length-composition data for that fleet.

For `length_bin` rows, the `length` column contains the lower edge of each length bin, the same as for length compositions. The `observed`, `age`, and `uncertainty` columns should usually be `NA`. The `fleet` column identifies which fleet or survey the length bins apply to, and `timing` can be `NA` unless fleet-specific timing is needed.

`length_bin` rows with `fleet = NA` and `timing = NA` set the population length bins instead. Growth uses these bins for the distribution of length at age, and the expected length compositions of each fleet are built from them. These rows never set fleet bins, even though `fleet = NA` means "shared by all fleets" for `age_to_length_conversion` rows. The population length bins must span every fleet's length bins, and no population bin can be wider than a fleet bin it overlaps. As for fleet bins, the last population bin is as wide as the bin before it. A population bin that crosses a fleet bin edge is split between the 2 fleet bins as if its fish were spread evenly within it, so fleet bin edges should also be population bin edges.

The first and last population length bins hold all smaller and all larger fish, so the last bin should start above the length of nearly all fish. Without these rows, FIMS uses bins 1 unit wide (1 mm for `data_big`) from the smallest fleet lower edge to the largest fleet upper edge, plus 1 more bin. Adding these rows can change weight at age, and so biomass, even without length compositions, because weight at age is then averaged over the length distribution at age. Population length bins need a growth module that gives length at age, so they are not used with `EWAA` growth.

```{r data_big-population-length-bins}
# population length bins 10 mm wide with lower edges from 0 to 1190 mm, which
# span the data_big fleet length bins (0 to 1150 mm)
population_length_bins <- tibble::tibble(
  type = "length_bin",
  fleet = NA_character_,
  age = NA_integer_,
  length = seq(0, 1190, by = 10),
  timing = NA_real_,
  observed = NA_real_,
  unit = NA_character_,
  uncertainty = NA_character_
)
data_with_population_bins <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  FIMS::data_big,
  population_length_bins
)
FIMSFrame(data_with_population_bins)
```

## Weight-at-age data (`type == "weight_at_age"`)

The weight-at-age data are not currently included in the likelihood and are just used for converting from numbers to biomass in the population dynamics. The `unit` column should be `mt` and the uncertainty should be `NA`.

Population weight-at-age rows should use `fleet = NA`. These values are used for total biomass, and also for spawning output unless separate `spawning_weight_at_age` rows are provided. They are also used as the default catch and index weights for any fleet that does not have its own weight-at-age data.

Rows with a fleet name provide the weight-at-age used for that fleet's catch and index calculations, such as weights measured from port samples or survey samples. For each year, FIMS uses values in this order: the fleet's own rows for that year, then that fleet's `timing = NA` rows, then the population weight-at-age rows. This means a fleet only needs to provide rows for years where its weights differ from the default. If there are no `fleet = NA` rows and only 1 fleet has weight-at-age rows, FIMS will use that fleet's rows as the population default, but it will issue a warning.

Rows with `timing = NA` are the default for every year, and rows with a `timing` replace that default for that year only. Timings outside the model years and the year after the last are an error. Every timing that is used needs 1 row for each model age, and rows are never averaged. Without `timing = NA` rows, every model year needs its own rows, plus the year after the last model year, because FIMS reports spawning biomass at the beginning of the year for every year, including the year after the last catches are removed from the population.

The weight-at-age observations for the `data_big` are identical across time steps and are provided for timing = 1 to 31 with `fleet = NA`. The same weights could be given as 1 set of rows with `timing = NA`.

```{r data_big-weight_at_age}
# first and last entries  of the weight-at-age data
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "weight_at_age") |>
  head(3)
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "weight_at_age") |>
  tail(3)

# check that the observations are identical across time steps within each age
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "weight_at_age") |>
  dplyr::group_by(age) |>
  dplyr::summarize(n_distinct = dplyr::n_distinct(observed))
```

```{r data_big-weight_at_age-plot}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Line plot showing weight at age showing identical monotonically increasing weight-at-age observations ages that are the same across time steps.
# plot of weight-at-age by time step
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "weight_at_age") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = age, y = observed)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(color = "blue") +
  ggplot2::xlab("Age") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Weight (mt)") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~timing) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = get_ages(data_4_model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  ggtitle("Weight-at-age by time step in data_big example data set")
```

## Maturity-at-age data (`type == "maturity_at_age"`)

Maturity-at-age data are optional. When they are present, `setup_default_parameters()` uses them in place of the default logistic maturity curve, and they are used as the proportion mature at age when calculating spawning output.

Each row gives the proportion mature (between 0 and 1) in the `observed` column for one age. The `unit` column must be `proportion` and the `fleet` must be `NA`, because maturity applies to the population rather than to a fleet. The `uncertainty` should be `NA`.

Maturity can be constant or vary by year:

  1. rows with `timing = NA` apply to every year, and
  2. rows with a `timing` replace those values for that year.

Maturity in the first model year also sets unfished spawning biomass per recruit, so it affects the stock--recruitment curve and the spawning biomass ratio in every year. Maturity in a later year changes spawning biomass in that year and, through the stock--recruitment relationship, recruitment in the following year.

Every model age needs a value for each `timing` that is used. Without `timing = NA` rows, every model year needs its own rows. As for weight-at-age data, so does the year after the last model year, because spawning output is calculated at the start of that year after the last catches are removed. Those rows do not add a model year. Projection years are model years, so they use their own rows or the `timing = NA` rows, not the maturity from the last data year.

`data_big` does not include maturity-at-age data. The example below adds a constant maturity ogive and a different ogive for the second year.

```{r data_big-maturity_at_age}
maturity_ages <- get_ages(data_4_model)
maturity_at_age <- tibble::tibble(
  type = "maturity_at_age",
  fleet = NA_character_,
  age = rep(maturity_ages, times = 2),
  length = NA_real_,
  timing = rep(
    c(NA, get_start_year(data_4_model) + 1),
    each = length(maturity_ages)
  ),
  observed = c(plogis(maturity_ages - 2), plogis(maturity_ages - 3)),
  unit = "proportion",
  uncertainty = NA_character_
)
data_with_maturity <- FIMSFrame(dplyr::bind_rows(data_big, maturity_at_age))
setup_default_Maturity(data_with_maturity, module_type = "Empirical") |>
  head(3)
```

## Spawning weight and fecundity (`type == "spawning_weight_at_age"` and `type == "fecundity_at_age"`)

Spawning output in each year is the sum over ages of numbers at age times proportion female, maturity, spawning weight at age, and fecundity at age. Each of the last 3 has a default, and rows for 1 of them replace the default for that factor only:

- Maturity comes from the maturity module. With `maturity_at_age` rows, `setup_default_parameters()` uses Empirical maturity, which takes its values from those rows.
- Spawning weight at age defaults to the population weight at age. It can be given separately, for example weight at the time of spawning.
- Fecundity at age defaults to 1. It is spawning output per unit of spawning weight, for example eggs per mt.

Without `spawning_weight_at_age` or `fecundity_at_age` rows, spawning output is spawning biomass. Both types are inputs for the population, so their rows need `fleet = NA`, and they use the same `timing` rule as weight at age: rows with `timing = NA` are the default for every year, rows with a `timing` replace that default for that year, and without `timing = NA` rows every model year and the year after the last need rows. The `unit` column describes the input, for example `mt` for spawning weight or `eggs/mt` for fecundity. Unfished spawning output and spawning output per recruit use the same product, with the values for the first model year for spawning output per recruit.

Because the 3 values are multiplied, a combined vector can be put in 1 of them with the others set to 1. For example, the Stock Synthesis empirical input of weight times maturity times eggs per weight can be entered as `fecundity_at_age`, with `spawning_weight_at_age` rows of 1 and `maturity_at_age` rows of 1 at every age. Stock Synthesis one-sex models count every fish as female, so also set `proportion_female = 1` (or the female fraction, `FracFemale_GP_1`, when the number of sexes is set to -1). The `spawning_biomass` output is then in the units of that vector.

## Fecundity at length (`type == "fecundity_at_length"`)

`fecundity_at_length` gives the spawning output of 1 fish in each population length bin, for example eggs per fish. FIMS averages it over the distribution of length at age, so it replaces spawning weight at age in spawning output. The `length` column gives the lower edge of each population length bin, and each timing needs 1 row for every population length bin. The rows need `fleet = NA` and follow the same `timing` rule as fecundity at age.

Fecundity at length needs population length bins (`length_bin` rows with `fleet = NA`) and growth that gives length at age, such as von Bertalanffy growth. With `EWAA` growth the rows are not used and FIMS warns. They cannot be combined with `spawning_weight_at_age` rows. `fecundity_at_age` rows still multiply spawning output, with a warning, so do not also use the combined-vector recipe above. Doubling fecundity at length doubles spawning output and unfished spawning output, so the spawning biomass ratio and recruitment do not change.

The Stock Synthesis fecundity options can be tabulated at the center of each population length bin, as Stock Synthesis does. Here `a` and `b` are the Stock Synthesis fecundity parameters, and `weight` is weight at the bin center in kg, the unit Stock Synthesis uses for fecundity. Options 4 and 5 can be negative for small fish, so they are set to 0. With length-based maturity in Stock Synthesis (maturity options 1 and 6), give maturity as `maturity_at_length`, described next.

```{r fecundity-at-length-ss3, eval = FALSE}
population_lengths <- seq(0, 1150, by = 50)
length_midpoints <- population_lengths + 25
weight <- length_weight_a * length_midpoints^length_weight_b
fecundity <- switch(ss3_fecundity_option,
  weight * (a + b * weight), # 1: eggs = weight x (a + b x weight)
  a * length_midpoints^b, # 2: eggs = a x length^b
  a * weight^b, # 3: eggs = a x weight^b
  pmax(a + b * length_midpoints, 0), # 4: eggs = a + b x length
  pmax(a + b * weight, 0) # 5: eggs = a + b x weight
)
fecundity_rows <- tibble::tibble(
  type = "fecundity_at_length",
  fleet = NA_character_,
  age = NA_real_,
  length = population_lengths,
  timing = NA_real_,
  observed = fecundity,
  unit = "eggs",
  uncertainty = NA_character_
)
```

## Maturity at length (`type == "maturity_at_length"`)

`maturity_at_length` gives the proportion mature in each population length bin. It follows the same rules as `fecundity_at_length`: rows need `fleet = NA`, 1 row for every population length bin in each timing, population length bins, and growth that gives length at age. As for `maturity_at_age`, values are from 0 to 1 and `unit = "proportion"`.

Spawning output at age is the sum over length bins of the probability of each length at that age times maturity at length times fecundity at length, or weight at the bin center without `fecundity_at_length`. This sum is then multiplied by maturity at age and fecundity at age. Maturity at length is applied inside the sum because a fish's maturity depends on its length. Applying a maturity at age after averaging over length would undercount the larger fish of an age. This matches how Stock Synthesis uses length-based maturity.

Maturity at age still multiplies the result. With `maturity_at_length` rows and no `maturity_at_age` rows, `setup_default_parameters()` sets maturity at age to 1 when growth gives length at age, and `setup_default_Maturity(data, module_type = "Empirical")` does the same. A maturity at age of only 0 and 1, such as Stock Synthesis's first mature age, can be combined with maturity at length. Values between 0 and 1 give a warning, because maturity would then be counted twice. Maturity parameters cannot be estimated. The `proportion_mature_at_age` output reports maturity at age only, not maturity at length.

A logistic maturity ogive in length can be tabulated at the bin centers:

```{r maturity-at-length-logistic, eval = FALSE}
population_lengths <- seq(0, 1150, by = 50)
length_midpoints <- population_lengths + 25
maturity_rows <- tibble::tibble(
  type = "maturity_at_length",
  fleet = NA_character_,
  age = NA_real_,
  length = population_lengths,
  timing = NA_real_,
  observed = 1 / (1 + exp(-slope * (length_midpoints - length_at_50_percent))),
  unit = "proportion",
  uncertainty = NA_character_
)
```

## Age-to-length conversion (`type == "age_to_length_conversion"`)

The age-to-length conversion data describe how individuals at each age are distributed across length bins. In this table, the `age` and `length` columns define every age-length bin combination, and the `observed` column gives the proportion (`unit = "proportion"`) or count (`unit = "number"`) of individuals at that age in each length bin. For each age, FIMS rescales the observed values so they sum to 1, and it warns when proportion inputs do not already sum to 1.

These data can be shared across fleets and years, or specified individually. Rows with `fleet = NA` are treated as shared across fleets that do not have fleet-specific information, while rows with `timing = NA` are treated as defaults across years that do not have their own timing. For a given fleet and year, FIMS uses rows in this order: (1) that fleet and year, (2) that fleet with `timing = NA`, (3) shared rows with `fleet = NA` for that year, and (4) shared rows with both `fleet = NA` and `timing = NA`. Each fleet-timing-age-length combination must appear at most once.

Age-to-length conversion data are not part of the likelihood. Instead, they are used in the population dynamics calculations to convert numbers at age to numbers at length when length-composition data are included and growth is not estimated internally.

Note: purely age-based models which have no length-composition data can omit the age-to-length conversion data as well.

```{r data_big-age_to_length_conversion}
# first and last entries in the age-to-length conversion data type
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_to_length_conversion") |>
  head(3)
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_to_length_conversion") |>
  tail(3)

# show that the number of rows in the age-to-length conversion data type is equal to the product of the number of unique combinations of age and length
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_to_length_conversion") |>
  nrow()
# 12 ages, 23 length bins:
length(unique(na.omit(FIMS::data_big$age))) * length(unique(na.omit(FIMS::data_big$length)))
```

```{r data_big-age_to_length_conversion-plot}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Scatter plot showing the age-to-length conversion with point size representing the proportion of fish at each age-length combination.
# plot of age-to-length conversion observations for the data_big example data set
FIMS::data_big |>
  dplyr::filter(type == "age_to_length_conversion") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(
      x = age,
      y = length,
      size = observed
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = gray(0, alpha = 0.3)) +
  ggplot2::scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.1, 12)) +
  ggplot2::xlab("Age") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Length (mm)") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = get_ages(data_4_model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  ggtitle("Age-to-length conversion for the data_big example data set")
```
